cim: Growing AI demand strains memory supply, triggering consumer shortages as giants seek more chips
cim_eredeti: Growing AI demand strains memory supply, triggering consumer shortages as giants seek more chips
szoveg_eredeti:
The growing computing and memory demands to train and run artificial intelligence (AI) models continue to elevate the importance of random-access memory (RAM) and high-bandwidth memory (HBM), straining the memory chip supply and sparking a debate over whether memory belongs in personal devices or in data centers.

RAM technology plays a key role in system performance as AI systems need it for memory and quick data transfers, which render RAM modules scarce in the consumer market.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman scrutinized the consumer need for RAM, which is an indispensable component for personal computers, in a recent podcast.

He argued that “it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM (dynamic random-access memory) sitting in their own computer and being used 5% of the time.”

Altman’s statement that memory is better used in data centers than in personal computers drew a sharp backlash on the internet, with even trillionaire Elon Musk pushing back on social media, saying that “the people deserve to have their own RAM, too.”

Altman later said his statements were taken out of context and that people could use as much RAM as they want, and that expanding memory production would be the real solution to the memory scarcity.

Yiran Chen, an electrical and computer engineering professor at Duke University, told Anadolu that RAM plays a key role in AI development as models are made up of massive neural networks with countless parameters that need to be stored in fast memory.

Chen said he disagrees with Altman’s statement that memory chips are better served in data centers, noting that not everything can be done through cloud computing due to privacy concerns, as consumers should be able to keep their data and process their data on their own devices.

He mentioned that the RAM debate is less about who gets the chips and more about who owns AI models and datasets, emphasizing that running AI models on personal computers will democratize the technology by reducing the need to rely on cloud providers.

He said similar discussions emerged during the rise of the internet, as some views at the time suggested that all computing would be moved to the cloud and personal computers would be no longer needed, which did not materialize.

Chen stressed that AI has to interact with the physical world, and that running models on devices like smartphones, self-driving vehicles, and wearables is becoming increasingly important.

He noted that running AI algorithms on a device already close to the data source offers shorter latency and higher reliability than on a central server at a data center. He added that smaller AI models are used on everyday devices and that these have lower energy consumption than AI servers, while offering reduced performance.

Chen said DRAM is not the only type of RAM used for AI systems, as VRAM in graphics processing units (GPUs) is faster and HBM is an even faster and specialized version of VRAM.

He added that manufacturers cannot scale up their production capacity in the short term and that there is a ramping competition in production capacity between memory used in personal computers and those used in high-end GPUs and central processing units (CPUs), which continue to fuel memory supply shortages and price hikes for consumers.
